q: The CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021 came into force:
opts: From the date of their publication in the Official Gazette
From the date the National Pension System Rules came into force
From 1 January 2021, the start of the year
From 1 April 2016, retrospectively
expl:
( A) From the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.
(B) From the date the National Pension System Rules came into force. — The two instruments are separate; rule 1(2) fixes this one's own date.
(C) From 1 January 2021, the start of the year. — The rules do not adopt a calendar date; they adopt the date of publication.
(D) From 1 April 2016, retrospectively. — There is no retrospective commencement in rule 1(2).

Rule 1(2) brings the rules into force with effect from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. They were notified by G.S.R. 868(E) dated 20 December 2021, so that is the commencement date. Notice the contrast with the 2016 Pay Rules, which were given retrospective effect from 1 January 2016: the pension rules have no such deeming provision, and a question that offers 1 January 2021 is trading on the wrong instrument.

Exam-safe point: Commencement: date of publication in the Gazette, 20.12.2021.

Statutory Authority: Rule 1(2), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Assuming a retrospective date as in the 2016 Pay Rules

q: The 2021 Rules apply to Government servants appointed:
opts: On or after 1 January 2004, because the rules are new
On or before 31 December 2003, in any establishment including a contributory one
On any date, whatever the date of appointment
On or before 31 December 2003, on a pensionable establishment
expl:
( D) On or before 31 December 2003, on a pensionable establishment.
(A) On or after 1 January 2004, because the rules are new. — That is the class the rules do NOT cover; post-2003 entrants are under the NPS Rules.
(B) On or before 31 December 2003, in any establishment including a contributory one. — Rule 2 expressly excludes persons entitled to a Contributory Provident Fund.
(C) On any date, whatever the date of appointment. — The cut-off date is central to rule 2, not incidental to it.

Rule 2 applies the rules to servants appointed on or before 31 December 2003, appointed substantively to civil services and posts borne on pensionable establishments. The cut-off is the whole architecture of the 2021 Rules: the same notification period also produced the CCS (Implementation of National Pension System) Rules, 2021, which govern those appointed after that date unless they fall in one of the Explanation cases.

Exam-safe point: Cut-off: 31.12.2003, and the establishment must be pensionable.

Statutory Authority: Rule 2, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Reading the 2021 date in the title as the cut-off

q: A servant was put on induction training in 2003 and appointed on a regular basis in 2004. Rule 2's Explanation:
opts: Excludes him, because the regular appointment was after the cut-off — The Explanation exists precisely to bring this case in
Excludes him unless he was paid a regular salary during training — A salary or a stipend suffices; a regular salary is not required
Covers him if the training was essential for the regular appointment and the training period counted as qualifying service
Covers him whatever the terms of the training — Three conditions attach, and all three must be met
expl:
( C) Covers him if the training was essential for the regular appointment and the training period counted as qualifying service.

Explanation (1) to rule 2 brings in a servant put on induction training on or before 31 December 2003 followed by regular appointment after that date, on three conditions: completion of the training was an essential condition for the regular appointment; he was eligible for a salary or a stipend during it; and the training period was eligible to count as qualifying service under the 1972 Rules. Miss any one and the Explanation does not reach him.

Exam-safe point: Induction training: three cumulative conditions, all in Explanation (1).

Statutory Authority: Rule 2, Explanation (1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Taking induction training as an automatic inclusion

q: The definition of 'gratuity' in rule 3(1)(o) includes:
opts: Retirement gratuity and commuted value of pension
Service gratuity, retirement or death gratuity, and residuary gratuity
Only service gratuity and retirement gratuity
Only retirement gratuity
expl:
( B) Service gratuity, retirement or death gratuity, and residuary gratuity.
(A) Retirement gratuity and commuted value of pension. — Commutation is pension, not gratuity.
(C) Only service gratuity and retirement gratuity. — Residuary gratuity under rule 45(3) is also inside the definition.
(D) Only retirement gratuity. — The definition is wider, and it names three instruments.

Rule 3(1)(o) defines gratuity to include service gratuity under rule 44, retirement or death gratuity under rule 45(1), and residuary gratuity under rule 45(3). The three are different instruments with different triggers: service gratuity replaces pension where qualifying service falls short; retirement and death gratuity are the lump sum on retirement or death; residuary gratuity fills up a shortfall where a pensioner dies within five years of retiring.

Exam-safe point: Three gratuities: service (r.44), retirement/death (r.45(1)), residuary (r.45(3)).

Statutory Authority: Rule 3(1)(o), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Treating 'gratuity' as a single instrument

q: A servant permanently transferred from a post not governed by these rules may elect to remain under his old pension rules. The option must be exercised:
opts: At any time before retirement — The option is time-bound, and the period runs from the transfer
Within six months of the order of permanent transfer, or of return from leave if on leave
Within three months of the transfer order, in every case
Within one year of the transfer order
expl:
( B) Within six months of the order of permanent transfer, or of return from leave if on leave.
(C) Within three months of the transfer order, in every case. — Three months is the voluntary-retirement notice period, not this option.
(D) Within one year of the transfer order. — The figure is six months, extended only for a servant on leave.

The proviso to rule 4(1) gives six months from the date of issue of the order of permanent transfer, or, if the servant is on leave on that date, six months from his return from leave, whichever is later. Rule 4(2) requires the option in writing to the authority making the transfer order, and rule 4(3) makes it final. Three separate sub-rules, three separate testable facts.

Exam-safe point: Option: six months, in writing, and final.

Statutory Authority: Rule 4, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Running the six months from the date of joining rather than the order

q: A servant's claim to pension is governed by:
opts: The rules in force when he retires, is retired, discharged, resigns or dies
Whichever set of rules is more beneficial to him
The rules in force when he was appointed
The rules in force on the date he applies for pension
expl:
( A) The rules in force when he retires, is retired, discharged, resigns or dies.
(B) Whichever set of rules is more beneficial to him. — Rule 5(1) fixes a single date; it offers no comparison.
(C) The rules in force when he was appointed. — Pension is governed by the rules at the exit, not the entry.
(D) The rules in force on the date he applies for pension. — The claim is judged at the event, not at the application.

Rule 5(1) is a choice-of-law provision: the claim is regulated by the provisions in force at the time the servant retires, is retired, is discharged, is allowed to resign, or dies. That is why the 1972 Rules still govern servants who retired before 20 December 2021, and why the 2021 Rules reach a retirement that happens after that date even where the service was rendered under the older rules.

Exam-safe point: Claim governed by the rules at the exit event.

Statutory Authority: Rule 5(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the rules in force at appointment

q: The day on which a servant retires, and the date of his death, are treated as:
opts: A half day, for pension arithmetic — The rule treats the day as completed, not as a fraction
A day of leave in every case
A day outside service, so no pay or qualifying service accrues
A completed working day — the last completed working day in the case of retirement
expl:
( D) A completed working day — the last completed working day in the case of retirement.
(B) A day of leave in every case. — Leave is the position only where he was in fact on leave immediately before.
(C) A day outside service, so no pay or qualifying service accrues. — Rule 5(2) does the opposite: it makes the day count.

Rule 5(2) treats the day of retirement or discharge as the last completed working day and the date of death as a completed working day. The proviso deals with the case where the servant was, immediately before, on leave or under suspension: then the day of retirement or death is part of that leave, absence or suspension. The point matters because a day more or less can move the ten-month average under rule 32.

Exam-safe point: Day of retirement or death counts as a completed day.

Statutory Authority: Rule 5(2), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Excluding the day of retirement from service

q: Under rule 6(1), a Government servant:
opts: Shall not earn two pensions even for wholly separate services
May always draw a second pension after re-employment
Shall not earn two pensions in the same service or post at the same time or by the same continuous service
May earn two pensions if the second is for a different post
expl:
( C) Shall not earn two pensions in the same service or post at the same time or by the same continuous service.
(A) Shall not earn two pensions even for wholly separate services. — The bar is confined to the same service or post and the same continuous service.
(B) May always draw a second pension after re-employment. — Re-employment is dealt with in rule 6(2) and is also barred, subject to rules 19 and 20.
(D) May earn two pensions if the second is for a different post. — The bar is on two pensions in the same service or post at the same time, not on two posts generally.

Rule 6(1) bars two pensions in the same service or post at the same time or by the same continuous service. Rule 6(2) then bars a separate pension or gratuity for a period of re-employment, except as provided in rule 19 or rule 20. The two sub-rules are often confused: (1) is about double-counting one service, (2) is about a pensioner who returns to Government service.

Exam-safe point: No two pensions for the same service or post at the same time.

Statutory Authority: Rule 6(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Reading rule 6(1) as a bar on all second pensions

q: Where a part of pension is withheld under rule 7(1)(b), the pension shall not be reduced below:
opts: Fifty per cent of the pension originally sanctioned
The amount of family pension admissible
The amount of minimum pension under rule 44
There is no floor; the whole pension may be withheld
expl:
( C) The amount of minimum pension under rule 44.
(A) Fifty per cent of the pension originally sanctioned. — The proviso fixes a floor by reference to rule 44, not a percentage.
(B) The amount of family pension admissible. — Family pension is a different instrument under rule 50.
(D) There is no floor; the whole pension may be withheld. — The whole may be withheld, but a part may not be reduced below the floor.

Rule 7(1)(b) allows the Appointing Authority to withhold or withdraw a pension, or part of it, permanently or for a specified period, where the pensioner is convicted of a serious crime or found guilty of grave misconduct. The proviso puts a floor under a partial withholding: the amount shall not be reduced below the minimum pension under rule 44. Withholding in full is a different power and is not touched by the proviso.

Exam-safe point: Partial withholding: never below the rule 44 minimum.

Statutory Authority: Rule 7(1)(b) and its proviso, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
src: Rule 7(1)(b) and its proviso, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the floor to a full withholding

q: A retired servant of an Intelligence organisation in the Second Schedule to the RTI Act publishes material on his work without clearance. The undertaking he gave was in:
opts: Form 3
Format 1
Format 2
Form 1
expl:
( B) Format 1.
(A) Form 3. — Form 3 is the nomination for gratuity.
(C) Format 2. — Format 2 is the President's sanction to institute proceedings after retirement.
(D) Form 1. — Form 1 is the application for commercial employment under rule 9; the undertaking is a Format.

The rulebook appends two separate series and rule 3 defines them separately: a Form is a form appended to the rules, and a Format is a format appended to them. Rule 7(4)(b) requires the undertaking to be given in Format 1, and a failure to observe it is treated as grave misconduct under rule 7. The distinction is worth learning as a pair, because the paper tests it by offering a Form where a Format is required.

Exam-safe point: Publication undertaking: Format 1, not Form 1.

Statutory Authority: Rules 3(1)(k), 3(1)(l) and 7(4)(b), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing the Form series with the Format series

q: Departmental proceedings not instituted while the servant was in service:
opts: May be instituted only with the sanction of the President, in Format 2
May never be instituted after retirement
May be instituted by any authority that could have done so in service
May be instituted for any event, however old
expl:
( A) May be instituted only with the sanction of the President, in Format 2.
(B) May never be instituted after retirement. — They may, on the conditions in rule 8(2)(c), which is why the sub-rule exists.
(C) May be instituted by any authority that could have done so in service. — The sanction of the President is a pre-condition, in Format 2.
(D) May be instituted for any event, however old. — Clause (ii) bars an event more than four years before the institution.

Rule 8(2)(c) sets three limits on proceedings not instituted in service: they shall not be instituted save with the sanction of the President in Format 2; they shall not concern an event more than four years before the institution; and they shall be conducted by such authority and place as the President directs. The proviso adds that a memorandum of charges must be communicated to the pensioner in Format 3.

Exam-safe point: Post-retirement proceedings: President's sanction, four-year bar, Formats 2 and 3.

Statutory Authority: Rule 8(2)(c), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Ignoring the four-year bar on the event

q: Where proceedings are pending, the provisional pension under rule 8(4)(a) is equal to:
opts: The minimum pension under rule 44
Fifty per cent of the pension, pending conclusion — There is no such fraction in rule 8(4)
Two-thirds of the pension that would have been admissible
The maximum pension that would have been admissible on the qualifying service up to retirement
expl:
( D) The maximum pension that would have been admissible on the qualifying service up to retirement.
(A) The minimum pension under rule 44. — The minimum is a floor elsewhere; here the amount is the maximum pension.
(C) Two-thirds of the pension that would have been admissible. — Two-thirds is the compulsory-retirement provisional figure under rule 40(3).

Rule 8(4)(a) authorises a provisional pension equal to the maximum pension that would have been admissible on the qualifying service up to the date of retirement — or, if the servant was under suspension on that date, up to the day before he was placed under suspension. This is the proceedings case, and it is deliberately generous because no gratuity is paid at all under rule 8(4)(c) until the proceedings conclude.

Exam-safe point: Proceedings case: maximum admissible pension, and no gratuity.

Statutory Authority: Rule 8(4), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing rule 8(4) with the rule 62 delay case

q: Where the President orders recovery of pecuniary loss from pension, the recovery shall not ordinarily exceed:
opts: Ten per cent of the pension
The whole pension, since it is a recovery of loss
One-half of the pension admissible on the date of retirement
One-third of the pension admissible on the date of retirement
expl:
( D) One-third of the pension admissible on the date of retirement.
(A) Ten per cent of the pension. — Ten per cent is the gratuity withholding in the rule 62 delay case.
(B) The whole pension, since it is a recovery of loss. — The rule caps the rate, which is the point of sub-rule (6).
(C) One-half of the pension admissible on the date of retirement. — The rule says one-third.

Rule 8(6) puts a rate cap on a recovery of pecuniary loss where the President decides not to withhold or withdraw the pension: the recovery shall not ordinarily be made at a rate exceeding one-third of the pension admissible on the date of retirement. The word 'ordinarily' leaves room for an exceptional case, but the starting rule is one-third.

Exam-safe point: Recovery cap: one-third of the pension at retirement.

Statutory Authority: Rule 8(6), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing the one-third recovery with the ten per cent withholding

q: A Group 'A' pensioner wishing to take up commercial employment must obtain sanction if he does so:
opts: Within six months of his retirement
At any time after retirement
Within one year of his retirement
Within two years of his retirement
expl:
( C) Within one year of his retirement.
(A) Within six months of his retirement. — Six months is the rule 4 option period.
(B) At any time after retirement. — The rule is confined to the first year; after that no sanction is required.
(D) Within two years of his retirement. — The period in rule 9(1) is one year.

Rule 9(1) requires a pensioner who was a member of Central Service Group 'A' immediately before retirement to obtain the previous sanction of the Government before accepting commercial employment within one year of retirement, applying in Form 1. Rule 9(8) supplies the sanction for breach: the Government may declare that he is not entitled to the whole or part of his pension for such period as the order specifies.

Exam-safe point: Commercial employment: one year, sanction in Form 1.

Statutory Authority: Rule 9(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Treating the bar as permanent

q: A Group 'A' pensioner accepting employment under a Government outside India without permission:
opts: Forfeits his pension permanently in every case
Forfeits pension for the period of that employment, or such longer period as the Government directs
Must refund his entire gratuity — The rule speaks of pension for the period, not of refunding gratuity
Suffers no consequence, because the pension is already sanctioned
expl:
( B) Forfeits pension for the period of that employment, or such longer period as the Government directs.
(A) Forfeits his pension permanently in every case. — The rule ties the loss to the period of employment, extendable by direction.
(D) Suffers no consequence, because the pension is already sanctioned. — Rule 10(1) attaches a consequence, and it is a period-based loss.

Rule 10(1) requires previous permission of the Central Government for employment under any Government outside India, and provides that no pension is payable in respect of any period for which he is so employed, or such longer period as the Government may direct. Read it against rule 9: rule 9 is commercial employment anywhere and carries a declaration power over pension; rule 10 is employment under a foreign Government and carries a period-based forfeiture.

Exam-safe point: Foreign Government employment: pension lost for the period.

Statutory Authority: Rule 10(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing the foreign-employment bar with the commercial-employment bar

q: A servant retires on superannuation after 33 years' qualifying service. His emoluments are ₹86,000 and his average emoluments ₹84,000. His pension under rule 44(1) is:
opts: ₹43,000 a month
₹1,25,000 a month, the ceiling
₹42,000 a month
₹86,000 a month, the last emoluments in full
expl:
( A) ₹43,000 a month.
(B) ₹1,25,000 a month, the ceiling. — The ceiling is not a rate; it caps a figure that reaches it.
(C) ₹42,000 a month. — That is 50 per cent of the average emoluments, which is the lower figure; the rule takes the more beneficial.
(D) ₹86,000 a month, the last emoluments in full. — The pension is 50 per cent of the emoluments, not the emoluments.

Rule 44(1) takes 50 per cent of emoluments or of average emoluments, whichever is more beneficial. Emoluments are ₹86,000, so 50 per cent is ₹43,000. Average emoluments are ₹84,000, so 50 per cent is ₹42,000. The larger is ₹43,000, and it lies between the floor of ₹9,000 and the ceiling of ₹1,25,000, so it is the pension.

Exam-safe point: Rule 44(1): 50% of the higher of emoluments and average emoluments.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Taking the average because it looks like the safer figure

q: A servant retires with ten years' qualifying service and emoluments of ₹16,000. His pension under rule 44(1) is:
opts: ₹9,000 a month, the minimum
₹8,000 a month
No pension is admissible below ₹20,000 of emoluments
₹16,000 a month
expl:
( A) ₹9,000 a month, the minimum.
(B) ₹8,000 a month. — That is 50 per cent of ₹16,000, but the rule puts a floor under it.
(C) No pension is admissible below ₹20,000 of emoluments. — There is no such threshold; the floor operates on the pension, not on the pay.
(D) ₹16,000 a month. — The pension is 50 per cent, not the full emoluments.

Fifty per cent of ₹16,000 is ₹8,000. Rule 44(1) fixes a minimum of ₹9,000 a month, so the pension is lifted to ₹9,000. The floor is on the amount of pension, not on the emoluments, so a question that offers a pay threshold has invented a rule.

Exam-safe point: Floor: ₹9,000 on the pension amount, not on the pay.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Leaving the pension at 50 per cent below the floor

q: A servant retires with emoluments of ₹3,00,000. His pension under rule 44(1) is:
opts: ₹2,50,000 a month
₹75,000 a month
₹1,50,000 a month
₹1,25,000 a month, the maximum
expl:
( D) ₹1,25,000 a month, the maximum.
(A) ₹2,50,000 a month. — That is not a figure in the rule at all.
(B) ₹75,000 a month. — Seventy-five thousand is the ordinary ceiling for family pension, not for pension.
(C) ₹1,50,000 a month. — That is 50 per cent of the emoluments, but the ceiling cuts it back.

Fifty per cent of ₹3,00,000 is ₹1,50,000, which is above the maximum of ₹1,25,000 a month fixed by rule 44(1). The pension is therefore ₹1,25,000. The ceiling and the floor are both in sub-rule (1), and the paper likes to offer the family pension ceiling of ₹75,000 alongside them.

Exam-safe point: Ceiling: ₹1,25,000 on pension; ₹75,000 belongs to family pension.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the family pension ceiling for the pension

q: A servant retires with exactly nine years and nine months of qualifying service. Under rule 44(8):
opts: He gets service gratuity, because he has less than ten years
His qualifying service is nine years and six months after rounding
His qualifying service is treated as ten years and he is eligible for pension
He gets nothing, because the minimum is ten years
expl:
( C) His qualifying service is treated as ten years and he is eligible for pension.
(A) He gets service gratuity, because he has less than ten years. — Sub-rule (8) exists to prevent exactly that result.
(B) His qualifying service is nine years and six months after rounding. — The rounding is upward to ten years, not downward.
(D) He gets nothing, because the minimum is ten years. — He is inside the sub-rule (8) rounding, so he is eligible.

Rule 44(8) provides that a servant who has rendered nine years and nine months or more but less than ten years shall have his qualifying service treated as ten years and shall be eligible for pension under sub-rule (1). Read it with rule 44(7), which treats a fraction of three months and above as a completed six-monthly period: the two together convert what looks like a shortfall into an entitlement.

Exam-safe point: 9 years 9 months or more: treat as 10, pension admissible.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(8), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Awarding service gratuity at nine years nine months

q: A servant retires after eight years of qualifying service with emoluments of ₹40,000. He is entitled to:
opts: Nothing, because he has not completed ten years
Service gratuity of ₹3,20,000
Pension of ₹20,000 a month
Retirement gratuity of ₹1,60,000
expl:
( B) Service gratuity of ₹3,20,000.
(A) Nothing, because he has not completed ten years. — Rule 44(2) gives service gratuity precisely for that case.
(C) Pension of ₹20,000 a month. — Pension needs ten years; eight years brings service gratuity.
(D) Retirement gratuity of ₹1,60,000. — That is the rule 45 computation; with under ten years it is service gratuity under rule 44(2).

Eight years is sixteen completed six-monthly periods. Rule 44(2) computes service gratuity at half a month's emoluments for every completed six-monthly period: ₹40,000 ÷ 2 = ₹20,000, times 16 = ₹3,20,000. This is the case rule 44(2) exists for — a servant who retires without reaching the ten years that pension requires.

Exam-safe point: Service gratuity: half a month's emoluments per six-monthly period.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(2), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the one-quarter retirement gratuity rate to service gratuity

q: A pensioner drawing a basic pension of ₹30,000 attains the age of 87. His additional pension is:
opts: ₹12,000 — 40 per cent of basic pension
₹9,000 — 30 per cent of basic pension
₹30,000 — 100 per cent of basic pension
₹6,000 — 20 per cent of basic pension
expl:
( B) ₹9,000 — 30 per cent of basic pension.
(A) ₹12,000 — 40 per cent of basic pension. — Forty per cent starts at 90.
(C) ₹30,000 — 100 per cent of basic pension. — One hundred per cent starts at 100 years.
(D) ₹6,000 — 20 per cent of basic pension. — Twenty per cent is the 80-to-85 band; at 87 he is in the 85-to-90 band.

Rule 44(6) adds a percentage of basic pension by age band: 20 per cent from 80 to under 85, 30 per cent from 85 to under 90, 40 per cent from 90 to under 95, 50 per cent from 95 to under 100, and 100 per cent at 100 or more. At 87 the band is 85 to 90, so the addition is 30 per cent of ₹30,000, which is ₹9,000. Sub-rule (6)(b) makes it payable from the first day of the month in which it falls due.

Exam-safe point: Additional pension bands: 20/30/40/50/100 per cent by age.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(6), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the 80-to-85 band for an 87-year-old

q: A servant has 27 years and 4 months of qualifying service. For pension, the qualifying service is treated as:
opts: 27 years and 6 months — the 4 months is a completed six-monthly period
28 years — the fraction rounds up to a full year
27 years and 4 months, counted to the month
27 years exactly — the fraction is ignored
expl:
( A) 27 years and 6 months — the 4 months is a completed six-monthly period.
(B) 28 years — the fraction rounds up to a full year. — The rounding is to a six-monthly period, not to a year.
(C) 27 years and 4 months, counted to the month. — Pension counts completed six-monthly periods, not months.
(D) 27 years exactly — the fraction is ignored. — Rule 44(7) does not ignore three months or more; it promotes it.

Rule 44(7) provides that in calculating the length of qualifying service, a fraction of a year equal to three months and above shall be treated as a completed six-monthly period. Four months is three months or above, so it becomes a six-monthly period, and the service is 27 years and 6 months — that is, 55 completed six-monthly periods. A fraction of less than three months would simply be dropped.

Exam-safe point: Three months or more: one more six-monthly period. Less than three: dropped.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(7), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Rounding the fraction to a whole year

q: A pension works out to ₹24,750.60. Under rule 44(9) it is expressed as:
opts: ₹24,750.60, carried to the paise
expl:
( D) ₹24,751.
(A) ₹24,750.60, carried to the paise. — The rule requires whole rupees.
(B) ₹24,750. — The rule rounds to the next higher rupee, not to the nearest.
(C) ₹24,760. — That rounds to the next ten rupees, which the rule does not do.

Rule 44(9) requires the amount finally determined to be expressed in whole rupees, and any fraction of a rupee to be rounded off to the next higher rupee. ₹24,750.60 therefore becomes ₹24,751. Note that this is rounding up, not rounding to the nearest: ₹24,750.10 would also become ₹24,751. Sub-rule (10) applies the same rounding where pension is discontinued mid-month.

Exam-safe point: Pension rounding: always to the next higher rupee.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(9), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Rounding to the nearest rupee

q: A servant retires after 32 years and 5 months of qualifying service with emoluments of ₹60,000. His retirement gratuity is:
opts: ₹9,90,000, the 16½-times cap
expl:
( C) ₹9,75,000.
(A) ₹4,87,500. — That uses one-eighth instead of one-quarter of emoluments.
(B) ₹9,90,000, the 16½-times cap. — The cap is the ceiling, not the computation; on these figures the computation is lower.
(D) ₹9,60,000. — That treats the 5 months as dropped; at three months or more it becomes a six-monthly period.

Thirty-two years and five months gives 64 completed six-monthly periods, plus one because rule 45(4) treats a fraction of three months or more as a completed six-monthly period — 65 in all. Rule 45(1)(a) pays one-fourth of emoluments per period: ₹60,000 ÷ 4 = ₹15,000, times 65 = ₹9,75,000. The cap is 16½ times emoluments, ₹9,90,000, which is not reached, so ₹9,75,000 is the gratuity.

Exam-safe point: Gratuity: one-quarter per six-monthly period, capped at 16½ times emoluments.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(1)(a) and (4), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Forgetting the cap, or forgetting the three-month rounding

q: A servant dies in service after 7 years and 2 months of qualifying service. His emoluments were ₹50,000. The death gratuity is:
expl:
( C) ₹6,00,000.
(A) ₹3,00,000. — That is the 2-times rate for under one year.
(B) ₹1,50,000. — That is the service gratuity pattern, not death gratuity.
(D) ₹10,00,000. — That is the 20-times rate for 11 years or more.

Seven years and two months is fourteen completed six-monthly periods. The table in rule 45(1)(b) gives 12 times emoluments for 5 years or more but less than 11 years. Twelve times ₹50,000 is ₹6,00,000, and it is below the ₹20 lakh ceiling, so that is the gratuity. The slabs are 2, 6, 12, 20 times, and then half of emoluments per completed period capped at 33 times.

Exam-safe point: Death gratuity slabs: 2 / 6 / 12 / 20 times, then half per period to 33.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(1)(b), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the 20-times slab for a seven-year servant

q: A servant dies in service after 21 years of qualifying service with emoluments of ₹70,000. The death gratuity is:
opts: ₹23,10,000, the 33-times cap
expl:
( B) ₹14,70,000.
(A) ₹14,00,000. — That is 20 times, which is the band below 20 years; at 21 years the half-per-period rate applies.
(C) ₹16,80,000. — That computes 24 periods rather than 21.
(D) ₹23,10,000, the 33-times cap. — The cap is not the rate; the computation gives less.

Twenty-one years is 42 completed six-monthly periods. At 20 years or more the table gives half of emoluments for every completed six-monthly period, subject to a maximum of 33 times emoluments: ₹70,000 ÷ 2 = ₹35,000, times 42 = ₹14,70,000. The cap of 33 times is ₹23,10,000, which is not reached, so the computation stands.

Exam-safe point: Top slab: half of emoluments per period, capped at 33 times.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(1)(b), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the 20-times slab above twenty years

q: The residuary gratuity under rule 45(3) is payable where a pensioner dies within five years of retirement and the sums received together with the retirement gratuity and commuted value fall short of:
opts: Twelve times his emoluments
Ten times his emoluments
Sixteen and a half times his emoluments
Thirty-three times his emoluments
expl:
( A) Twelve times his emoluments.
(B) Ten times his emoluments. — The figure in rule 45(3) is twelve.
(C) Sixteen and a half times his emoluments. — That is the retirement gratuity cap, not the residuary benchmark.
(D) Thirty-three times his emoluments. — That is the death gratuity cap.

Rule 45(3) measures the shortfall against twelve times his emoluments. If the pension and gratuity actually received, together with the retirement gratuity and the commuted value of any commuted portion, come to less than twelve times emoluments, a residuary gratuity equal to the deficiency is paid to the family. The figure to hold is twelve, and it is a benchmark for this one calculation only.

Exam-safe point: Residuary gratuity: the deficiency below twelve times emoluments.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(3), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the 16½ or 33 times caps as the residuary benchmark

q: A servant retires with four years and nine months of qualifying service. For retirement gratuity under rule 45(5):
opts: He gets service gratuity only, because he is below five years
He gets nothing, because five years is the minimum
His service is rounded down to four years — The rounding is upward, to five years
His qualifying service is treated as five years and he is eligible for retirement gratuity
expl:
( D) His qualifying service is treated as five years and he is eligible for retirement gratuity.
(A) He gets service gratuity only, because he is below five years. — Sub-rule (5) treats him as having five years for this purpose.
(B) He gets nothing, because five years is the minimum. — The minimum is reached by the deeming in sub-rule (5).

Rule 45(5) provides that a servant who has rendered four years and nine months or more but less than five years shall have his qualifying service treated as five years for the purpose of this rule and shall be eligible for retirement gratuity under clause (a) of sub-rule (1). It mirrors rule 44(8), which does the same at nine years nine months for pension. The pattern to learn is the nine-month shortfall, at both thresholds.

Exam-safe point: 4 years 9 months = 5 years for gratuity; 9 years 9 months = 10 years for pension.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(5), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing the two nine-month concessions

q: A servant dies in service leaving a widow. His pay for family pension is ₹60,000. After the enhanced period ends, the family pension is:
opts: ₹75,000 a month — the maximum
₹9,000 a month — the minimum
₹30,000 a month — 50 per cent of pay
₹18,000 a month — 30 per cent of pay
expl:
( D) ₹18,000 a month — 30 per cent of pay.
(A) ₹75,000 a month — the maximum. — The maximum applies only where 30 per cent exceeds it.
(B) ₹9,000 a month — the minimum. — The minimum applies only where 30 per cent falls below it.
(C) ₹30,000 a month — 50 per cent of pay. — Fifty per cent is the enhanced rate, which runs for ten years and then steps down.

Rule 50(2)(a)(i) sets the ordinary family pension at 30 per cent of pay, subject to a minimum of ₹9,000 and a maximum of ₹75,000 a month. Thirty per cent of ₹60,000 is ₹18,000. The enhanced rate under sub-clause (ii) is 50 per cent, but it is payable for ten years from the death and then the pension reverts to the sub-clause (i) rate under clause (b).

Exam-safe point: Family pension: 30% normal, 50% enhanced for ten years.

Statutory Authority: Rule 50(2), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the enhanced rate beyond its period

q: A servant dies in service. His pay for family pension is ₹2,00,000. The enhanced family pension is:
opts: ₹1,25,000 a month, the maximum
₹75,000 a month
₹1,00,000 a month
₹60,000 a month
expl:
( C) ₹1,00,000 a month.
(A) ₹1,25,000 a month, the maximum. — The maximum applies only if 50 per cent exceeds it; 50 per cent of ₹2,00,000 is ₹1,00,000.
(B) ₹75,000 a month. — That is the ordinary ceiling, not the enhanced one.
(D) ₹60,000 a month. — That is 30 per cent, the ordinary rate.

Fifty per cent of ₹2,00,000 is ₹1,00,000. The enhanced family pension under rule 50(2)(a)(ii) is 50 per cent of pay, and sub-clause (iv) puts its ceiling at ₹1,25,000. ₹1,00,000 is below that ceiling, so it stands. Had the pay been ₹3,00,000, the figure would have been cut to the ₹1,25,000 ceiling.

Exam-safe point: Enhanced family pension ceiling: ₹1,25,000.

Statutory Authority: Rule 50(2)(a)(ii) and (iv), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the ₹75,000 ordinary ceiling for the enhanced rate

q: A pensioner dies after retirement. The enhanced family pension is payable for:
opts: For life — The enhanced rate is time-bound; the ordinary rate follows it
Seven years, or until he would have attained 67, whichever is less
Ten years, as on a death in service
Seven years in every case
expl:
( B) Seven years, or until he would have attained 67, whichever is less.
(C) Ten years, as on a death in service. — Ten years is the death-in-service period under sub-clause (ii).
(D) Seven years in every case. — The seven years is cut short if he would have reached 67 sooner.

Rule 50(2)(a)(iii) gives the enhanced family pension after a death following retirement for seven years, or up to the date the deceased pensioner would have attained sixty-seven years had he survived, whichever is less. Two provisos then cap it: it shall not exceed the pension authorised on retirement, and where that pension is below the ordinary family pension rate, the family pension is limited to the ordinary rate.

Exam-safe point: After retirement: seven years or age 67 of the pensioner, whichever is less.

Statutory Authority: Rule 50(2)(a)(iii), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the ten-year death-in-service period after retirement

q: A servant dies in service with pay for family pension of ₹22,000. The ordinary family pension is:
opts: ₹9,000 a month, the minimum
₹6,600 a month
₹11,000 a month
Nothing, because the pay is too low
expl:
( A) ₹9,000 a month, the minimum.
(B) ₹6,600 a month. — That is 30 per cent, but the rule puts a floor under it.
(C) ₹11,000 a month. — That is 50 per cent, the enhanced rate.
(D) Nothing, because the pay is too low. — The floor guarantees a minimum, whatever the pay.

Thirty per cent of ₹22,000 is ₹6,600, which is below the minimum of ₹9,000 fixed by rule 50(2)(a)(i). The family pension is therefore ₹9,000. The same floor of ₹9,000 applies to the enhanced rate under sub-clause (iv), so even the 50 per cent figure cannot fall below it.

Exam-safe point: Family pension floor: ₹9,000, on both the ordinary and enhanced rates.

Statutory Authority: Rule 50(2)(a)(i), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Leaving the family pension below the floor

q: Under rule 50(6), the order in which family pension is payable is:
opts: Widow or widower, then children, then dependent parents, then dependent disabled siblings
All eligible members in equal shares at the same time, always
Children first, then widow or widower — The widow or widower comes first
Widow or widower, then parents, then children — Children come before parents
expl:
( A) Widow or widower, then children, then dependent parents, then dependent disabled siblings.
(B) All eligible members in equal shares at the same time, always. — Rule 50(7)(a) makes it payable to one member at a time, save in the listed cases.

Rule 50(6) sets a four-step order: the widow or widower (including a post-retiral spouse and a judicially separated spouse); then children, including adopted and step children and children born after retirement; then dependent parents; then dependent siblings suffering from a mental or physical disability. Rule 50(7)(a) adds that it is not payable to more than one member at a time, subject to the listed exceptions where it is shared.

Exam-safe point: Order: spouse, children, dependent parents, dependent disabled siblings.

Statutory Authority: Rule 50(6) and (7), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Putting children ahead of the spouse

q: A son of a deceased servant, not suffering from any disability, is eligible for family pension if he is:
opts: Unmarried, at any age, if he is a student
Below eighteen, the age of majority
Below twenty-one and unmarried — The age is twenty-five
Unmarried, below twenty-five, and not earning his livelihood
expl:
( D) Unmarried, below twenty-five, and not earning his livelihood.
(A) Unmarried, at any age, if he is a student. — There is no student concession; the age limit is absolute for a son without disability.
(B) Below eighteen, the age of majority. — Eighteen is the age of majority, not the family pension limit.

Rule 50(9)(a)(i) makes an ordinary son eligible only if he is unmarried, below twenty-five years and not earning his livelihood. Clause (ii) does the same for a daughter, but permits her to be unmarried, widowed or divorced — the daughter is not required to be unmarried. A son or daughter suffering from a mental or physical disability under clause (iii) has no age limit, and receives it for life on the conditions in clause (h).

Exam-safe point: Son: unmarried, under 25, not earning. Daughter: unmarried, widowed or divorced.

Statutory Authority: Rule 50(9)(a), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the same marital condition to sons and daughters

q: The rules define a 'Form' and a 'Format' separately. Which is correct?
opts: They are synonyms, and either word may be used for any appendix
A Format is a form prescribed by a State Government — Nothing in the definition ties a Format to a State
A Form is a form appended to the rules; a Format is a format appended to them — two separate series
A Form is used in service, a Format after retirement
expl:
( C) A Form is a form appended to the rules; a Format is a format appended to them — two separate series.
(A) They are synonyms, and either word may be used for any appendix. — Rules 3(1)(k) and 3(1)(l) define them in two separate clauses.
(D) A Form is used in service, a Format after retirement. — The distinction is by appendix, not by stage of service.

Rule 3(1)(k) defines a Form as a form appended to these rules; rule 3(1)(l) defines a Format as a format appended to them. The two series are appended separately and are numbered independently, which is why the rules can speak of Form 3 (nomination) and Format 3 (memorandum of charges) without confusion. When a question asks which instrument is prescribed, the answer depends on the clause, and the clause says Form or Format.

Exam-safe point: Form and Format are two distinct appended series.

Statutory Authority: Rules 3(1)(k) and 3(1)(l), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Treating Form and Format as interchangeable

q: A Government servant, on initial appointment, makes a nomination for retirement and death gratuity in:
opts: Form 1
Form 3
Form 9
Format 3
expl:
( B) Form 3.
(A) Form 1. — Form 1 is the application for commercial employment.
(C) Form 9. — Form 9 is the claim a family member submits for gratuity.
(D) Format 3. — Format 3 is the memorandum of charges to a pensioner under rule 8.

Rule 46(1) requires a Government servant, on his initial appointment, to make a nomination in Form 3 conferring on one or more persons the right to receive the retirement gratuity and death gratuity payable under rule 45. The nomination goes to the Head of Office, who verifies and countersigns it under rule 46(9)(b) and has an entry made in the service book.

Exam-safe point: Nomination: Form 3, filed on initial appointment.

Statutory Authority: Rule 46(1), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Answering Format 3 for the nomination

q: A memorandum of charges to be communicated to a pensioner under rule 8 is in:
opts: Form 3
Format 3
Form 9
Format 1
expl:
( B) Format 3.
(A) Form 3. — Form 3 is the nomination for gratuity, which is a very different document.
(C) Form 9. — Form 9 is a family member's claim for gratuity.
(D) Format 1. — Format 1 is the intelligence organisation's publication undertaking.

The proviso to rule 8(2)(c) requires the memorandum of charges to be communicated to the pensioner in Format 3. The Formats are the working papers of the proceedings side of the rules — the sanction to institute proceedings is Format 2, the charges are Format 3 — while the Forms belong mostly to the claims and certificates side.

Exam-safe point: Charges memorandum: Format 3. Sanction: Format 2.

Statutory Authority: Rule 8(2)(c) proviso, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Reaching for Form 3 because it is the better-known number

q: The undertaking on post-retirement publication, required of a servant of an Intelligence organisation, is in:
opts: Format 1
Form 2
Form 1
Format 4
expl:
( A) Format 1.
(B) Form 2. — Form 2 is the check list for commercial employment.
(C) Form 1. — Form 1 begins the commercial-employment process.
(D) Format 4. — Format 4 is the certificate of qualifying service.

Rule 7(4)(b) requires the undertaking in Format 1. A failure to observe it is treated as grave misconduct under rule 7, which is why the undertaking is a statutory document and not an internal formality. In a case of a servant transferred out of such an organisation, rule 7(4)(c) requires the undertaking in duplicate, one copy in the service book and one kept by the organisation.

Exam-safe point: Publication undertaking: Format 1, and in duplicate on transfer.

Statutory Authority: Rule 7(4)(b) and (c), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Answering Form 1 for the undertaking

q: The Head of Office communicates the qualifying service determined at verification to the servant in:
opts: Format 6
Format 5
Form 4
Format 4
expl:
( D) Format 4.
(A) Format 6. — Format 6 is the medical certificate of incapacity.
(B) Format 5. — Format 5 is the relieving order on absorption in a State Government.
(C) Form 4. — Form 4 is the particulars-of-family form.

Rule 30(1) requires the Head of Office, in consultation with the Accounts Officer, to verify service and communicate the qualifying service determined in Format 4 on two occasions: after eighteen years of service, and when five years of service remain before superannuation. Rule 30(4) makes that verification final and not open to reopening except on a change in the rules.

Exam-safe point: Qualifying service certificate: Format 4, at 18 years and at 5 years to go.

Statutory Authority: Rule 30(1) and (4), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Answering Form 4 for the certificate

q: The medical authority's certificate of incapacity for service, leading to invalid pension, is issued in:
opts: Format 3
Form 6
Format 6
Form 5
expl:
( C) Format 6.
(A) Format 3. — Format 3 is the memorandum of charges.
(B) Form 6. — Form 6 is a different instrument again; the incapacity certificate is a Format.
(D) Form 5. — Form 5 is a medical certificate, but under the leave rules, not this one.

Rule 39(8) requires the medical authority to issue a Medical Certificate in Format 6, and if the servant is found unfit for further service, invalid pension may be granted under rule 44 not later than forty five days from the receipt of that certificate. The forty-five-day period is the testable figure: it runs from the receipt of the Format 6 certificate, not from the application.

Exam-safe point: Incapacity certificate: Format 6; invalid pension within 45 days of receipt.

Statutory Authority: Rule 39(8), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing Format 6 with the leave rules' Form 5

q: A pensioner applying for sanction to take up commercial employment applies in:
opts: Format 2
Format 1
Form 1
Form 5
expl:
( C) Form 1.
(A) Format 2. — Format 2 is the President's sanction to institute proceedings.
(B) Format 1. — Format 1 is the publication undertaking.
(D) Form 5. — Form 5 is not the right series for this; the application is a Form, and it is Form 1.

Rule 9(1) requires the application to be made in Form 1, and rule 9(5) requires the administrative Ministry to maintain a check list in Form 2. The two Form numbers sit next to each other and belong to the same procedure: the pensioner applies in Form 1 and the Ministry works the case on the Form 2 check list. A question that offers Format 1 is testing whether you noticed the word.

Exam-safe point: Commercial employment: application in Form 1, check list in Form 2.

Statutory Authority: Rules 9(1) and 9(5), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Answering Format 1 for the application

q: Where there is no natural guardian, up to twenty per cent of a minor's share of gratuity may be paid on:
opts: A succession certificate
An indemnity bond in Format 7
An affidavit sworn before a Magistrate
A guardianship certificate, which is always required
expl:
( B) An indemnity bond in Format 7.
(A) A succession certificate. — A succession certificate is the rule 49 route where there is no family and no nomination.
(C) An affidavit sworn before a Magistrate. — The instrument is an indemnity bond, and it is a Format.
(D) A guardianship certificate, which is always required. — The rule 47(7) procedure exists to allow payment without one, up to twenty per cent.

Rule 47(7) allows payment of an amount not exceeding twenty per cent of the minor's share to a guardian without a guardianship certificate, on an indemnity bond in Format 7; the balance follows on production of the certificate of guardianship. Rule 47(6) prefers the natural guardian, and rule 47(5) makes the payment to the guardian on the minor's behalf.

Exam-safe point: Minor's gratuity: 20 per cent on a Format 7 indemnity bond, balance on guardianship certificate.

Statutory Authority: Rule 47(5) to (7), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Removing the twenty per cent ceiling

q: Qualifying service commences from the date the Government servant:
opts: takes charge of the post to which he is first appointed, substantively or in an officiating or temporary capacity
attains the age of eighteen years, in every case
completes the probation period attached to his first post
is confirmed in his first appointment — Confirmation is dealt with at rule 16; commencement is at rule 11
expl:
( A) takes charge of the post to which he is first appointed, substantively or in an officiating or temporary capacity.
(B) attains the age of eighteen years, in every case. — Service before eighteen is excluded by the second proviso, with a military-service exception.
(C) completes the probation period attached to his first post. — Rule 16 separately provides that probation followed by confirmation qualifies.

Rule 11 fixes commencement at the date of taking charge of the post to which the servant is first appointed, whether substantively, in an officiating capacity or on a temporary basis. Two provisos qualify it: officiating or temporary service must be followed without interruption by substantive appointment, and service before the age of eighteen does not count except in the case of military service counted for civil pension under rule 20.

Exam-safe point: Qualifying service begins on taking charge, not on confirmation.

Statutory Authority: Rule 11, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Reading confirmation or probation into the commencement date

q: Service as an apprentice counts as qualifying service:
opts: never, under any circumstances — There is an express exception for SAS apprentices in the two accounts departments
only where the apprentice was subsequently confirmed
in every case, because apprenticeship is a recognised form of service — Rule 17 is a rule of exclusion, not inclusion
only in the case of a Subordinate Accounts Service apprentice in the IA&AD or the Defence Accounts Department
expl:
( D) only in the case of a Subordinate Accounts Service apprentice in the IA&AD or the Defence Accounts Department.
(B) only where the apprentice was subsequently confirmed. — The exception is by department and service, not by later confirmation.

Rule 17 states the general rule first: service as an apprentice shall not qualify. It then carves out the Subordinate Accounts Service apprentice in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department or the Defence Accounts Department. The examinable point is the narrowness of the exception, which sits alongside rule 16, where service on probation followed by confirmation does qualify.

Exam-safe point: Apprenticeship: excluded, except SAS apprentices in IA&AD and Defence Accounts.

Statutory Authority: Rules 16 and 17, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Generalising the SAS exception to all apprentices

topic: Leave that counts as qualifying service
q: Which leave counts as qualifying service without any special order?
opts: Only earned leave and half pay leave
No leave at all counts; only duty counts
All extraordinary leave, whatever the reason for which it was granted
All leave for which leave salary is payable, and all extraordinary leave granted on medical certificate
expl:
( D) All leave for which leave salary is payable, and all extraordinary leave granted on medical certificate.
(A) Only earned leave and half pay leave. — Leave salary is the test, which also covers commuted leave and leave not due.
(B) No leave at all counts; only duty counts. — Rule 21 is an inclusive provision and expressly counts leave with salary.
(C) All extraordinary leave, whatever the reason for which it was granted. — Ordinary extraordinary leave counts only if the appointing authority so allows at the time of grant.

Rule 21 counts all leave during service for which leave salary is payable and all extraordinary leave granted on medical certificate. The proviso allows the appointing authority, at the time of granting other extraordinary leave, to direct that it count where the servant could not join or rejoin duty because of civil commotion or was prosecuting higher scientific and technical studies.

Exam-safe point: Leave with salary and medical-certificate EOL count; other EOL does not unless allowed on grant.

Statutory Authority: Rule 21, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Counting all extraordinary leave as qualifying

q: Time under suspension counts as qualifying service where, on conclusion of the inquiry, the servant:
opts: has the period regularised as extraordinary leave
is reinstated, whatever the findings — Reinstatement is not the test; the findings on the inquiry are
is fully exonerated, or only a minor penalty is imposed and the suspension is held wholly unjustified
is awarded any penalty short of dismissal
expl:
( C) is fully exonerated, or only a minor penalty is imposed and the suspension is held wholly unjustified.
(A) has the period regularised as extraordinary leave. — Regularising it as extraordinary leave is a different consequence under rule 27.
(D) is awarded any penalty short of dismissal. — The rule requires exoneration, or a minor penalty with an unjustified suspension.

Rule 23(1) counts suspension time only where the servant is fully exonerated, or where only a minor penalty is imposed and the suspension is held to be wholly unjustified. Rule 23(2) otherwise excludes it unless the competent authority expressly declares that it shall count, and rule 23(3) requires that declaration to be made by order and recorded in the service book.

Exam-safe point: Suspension counts only on exoneration, or a minor penalty with unjustified suspension.

Statutory Authority: Rule 23, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Assuming any reinstatement makes suspension count

q: A Government servant resigns to take up an appointment in a private commercial company. He later asks to withdraw the resignation. The appointing authority:
opts: may accept it with the President's approval
shall not accept the request, because the resignation was to join a private commercial company
may accept it if a comparable post is available
may accept it if the absence did not exceed ninety days
expl:
( B) shall not accept the request, because the resignation was to join a private commercial company.
(A) may accept it with the President's approval. — Rule 26(6) is an absolute bar, not a matter of higher sanction.
(C) may accept it if a comparable post is available. — Availability of the post is one of the rule 26(5) conditions, which rule 26(6) overrides.
(D) may accept it if the absence did not exceed ninety days. — The ninety-day condition in rule 26(5)(iii) cannot rescue a resignation of this kind.

Rule 26(5) permits withdrawal in the public interest on four conditions, including absence of not more than ninety days and availability of the post. Rule 26(6) then bars withdrawal altogether where the resignation was tendered to take up an appointment in a private commercial company, or in a corporation or company owned or controlled by the Government, or in a body controlled or financed by it.

Exam-safe point: Withdrawal is barred where the resignation was to join a company or body.

Statutory Authority: Rule 26(5) and (6), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Applying the ninety-day rule to a barred category

q: An interruption in service forfeits past service, except in which case?
opts: Joining time while on transfer from one post to another
Dismissal followed by reinstatement on review
Unauthorised absence after the post has been filled substantively
Resignation accepted to join another Government post without permission
expl:
( A) Joining time while on transfer from one post to another.
(B) Dismissal followed by reinstatement on review. — Reinstatement restores past service under rule 25, but the dismissal itself was not an excepted interruption.
(C) Unauthorised absence after the post has been filled substantively. — Clause (b) protects unauthorised absence in continuation of authorised leave only while the post is not filled substantively.
(D) Resignation accepted to join another Government post without permission. — Rule 26 governs resignation, and the protection in rule 26(2) requires proper permission.

Rule 27(1) lists five exceptions to forfeiture: authorised leave of absence; unauthorised absence in continuation of authorised leave so long as the post is not filled substantively; suspension immediately followed by reinstatement, or ending in death or retirement; transfer to non-qualifying service in the public interest; and joining time on transfer. Rule 27(2) then lets the appointing authority commute periods of absence without leave retrospectively into extraordinary leave.

Exam-safe point: Joining time is an excepted interruption.

Statutory Authority: Rule 27, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Treating any absence as an excepted interruption

q: Verification of qualifying service under rule 30 is:
opts: final, and not to be reopened except on a subsequent change in the rules or orders governing qualifying service
open to reopening at any time on audit objection — Only a change in the governing rules and orders reopens it
provisional until the pension case is settled — Rule 30(4) makes the verification final, not provisional
final only where the servant has completed eighteen years
expl:
( A) final, and not to be reopened except on a subsequent change in the rules or orders governing qualifying service.
(D) final only where the servant has completed eighteen years. — The eighteen-year point is one of the two occasions for verification, not a condition of finality.

Rule 30(1) requires verification after eighteen years of service and again when five years remain before superannuation, with the result communicated in Format 4. Rule 30(4) makes the verification final and immune from reopening except where a subsequent change in the rules and orders governing the conditions under which service qualifies for pension necessitates it.

Exam-safe point: Verification is final; only a change of rules reopens it.

Statutory Authority: Rule 30(1) and (4), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Treating the Format 4 certificate as provisional

topic: Average emoluments across a broken month
q: A servant retires on 16 July 2019. For the fractional periods of the last ten months, emoluments are computed:
opts: by ignoring the fractional periods altogether
by taking the actual number of days in each calendar month as the denominator
by rounding each fraction up to a whole month
by multiplying the emolument by 14/30 and 16/30, whatever the number of days in the month
expl:
( D) by multiplying the emolument by 14/30 and 16/30, whatever the number of days in the month.
(A) by ignoring the fractional periods altogether. — The rule includes equal periods before the ten months so that fractions add to a full month.
(B) by taking the actual number of days in each calendar month as the denominator. — The rule fixes a thirty-day month precisely to avoid that.
(C) by rounding each fraction up to a whole month. — Rounding up belongs to rule 44(9), and to the amount of pension, not to average emoluments.

Rule 32(3) provides that where leave without salary or suspension not counting as service falls within the last ten months, the period is disregarded and an equal period before the ten months is included, a month being reckoned as thirty days so that fractions add up to a full month. The illustration works the point: a retirement on 16 July 2019 gives fractional periods of fourteen days of September 2018 and sixteen days of July 2019, computed at 14/30 and 16/30, including for February.

Exam-safe point: Thirty-day month: 14/30 and 16/30, even for February.

Statutory Authority: Rule 32(3) and its Illustration, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
src: Rule 32(3) and its Illustration, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the calendar month as the denominator

q: Pay drawn while on deputation to a State Government is:
opts: ignored altogether for pension purposes — It is not ignored; the counterfactual Central pay is substituted for it
treated as emoluments only if the deputation exceeded one year — There is no duration condition in rule 31(7)
not treated as emoluments; the pay he would have drawn under the Central Government is treated as emoluments
treated as emoluments, because it is the pay actually drawn
expl:
( C) not treated as emoluments; the pay he would have drawn under the Central Government is treated as emoluments.
(D) treated as emoluments, because it is the pay actually drawn. — Actual drawal does not decide the question; rule 31(6) and 31(7) split ex-cadre from State deputation.

Rule 31(6) treats pay drawn on deputation to an ex-cadre post in the same or another Central Government Department, or to the Armed Forces, as emoluments. Rule 31(7) draws the opposite conclusion for deputation to a State Government or foreign service: that pay is not emoluments, and the pay the servant would have drawn under the Central Government is treated as emoluments instead.

Exam-safe point: State deputation: substitute the Central pay; ex-cadre: actual pay counts.

Statutory Authority: Rules 31(6) and 31(7), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing ex-cadre deputation with State deputation

q: For the calculation of retirement benefits, a stagnation increment is:
opts: excluded, because it is not basic pay
treated as emoluments
included only where it was actually drawn for ten months
included only for gratuity, not for pension
expl:
( B) treated as emoluments.
(A) excluded, because it is not basic pay. — The Explanation to rule 31(1) expressly includes it.
(C) included only where it was actually drawn for ten months. — The ten-month averaging is a rule 32 question, not a condition on the Explanation.
(D) included only for gratuity, not for pension. — The Explanation speaks of retirement benefits generally.

Rule 31(1) defines emoluments as basic pay under rule 9(21)(a)(i) of the Fundamental Rules immediately before retirement or on the date of death, and adds non-practising allowance for a medical officer in lieu of private practice. The Explanation then provides that a stagnation increment shall be treated as emoluments for the calculation of retirement benefits.

Exam-safe point: Stagnation increment counts as emoluments.

Statutory Authority: Rule 31(1) and its Explanation, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
src: Rule 31(1) and its Explanation, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Treating the stagnation increment as outside basic pay

q: For a non-Gazetted servant whose pay exceeds ₹54,000 a month, the medical authority for invalid pension is:
opts: any authorised medical attendant
a Medical Board
the Civil Surgeon alone
a District Medical Officer alone
expl:
( B) a Medical Board.
(A) any authorised medical attendant. — The attendant appears in the leave rules, not here.
(C) the Civil Surgeon alone. — The Civil Surgeon route is for the other cases in rule 39(3)(b).
(D) a District Medical Officer alone. — The District Medical Officer is within clause (b), not clause (a).

Rule 39(3) fixes the authority by clause (a) and clause (b): a Medical Board for a Gazetted servant and for a non-Gazetted servant whose pay under rule 9(21) of the Fundamental Rules exceeds fifty-four thousand rupees a month; and the Civil Surgeon, a District Medical Officer, or a Medical Officer of equivalent status in other cases. Rule 39(7) adds that a lady doctor shall sit on the Board when a woman is examined.

Exam-safe point: Medical Board above ₹54,000 and for all Gazetted servants.

Statutory Authority: Rule 39(3) and (7), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the pay threshold only for non-Gazetted staff

q: Where a servant is dismissed, the competent authority must decide on a compassionate allowance:
opts: not later than three months after the order imposing the penalty
at any time before the servant attains superannuation
only if the servant applies within ninety days
within six months of the order, in every case
expl:
( A) not later than three months after the order imposing the penalty.
(B) at any time before the servant attains superannuation. — Rule 41(2) sets a three-month limit.
(C) only if the servant applies within ninety days. — The authority must act on its own motion or on the representation, within the same three months.
(D) within six months of the order, in every case. — Six months is the rule 41(4) period, and only for penalties imposed before the rules commenced.

Rule 41(1) forfeits pension and gratuity on dismissal or removal, subject to a compassionate allowance not exceeding two-thirds of the pension or gratuity that would have been admissible on superannuation retirement. Rule 41(2) requires the competent authority to decide the question on its own motion or on the servant's representation not later than three months after the penalty order. Rule 41(4) gives six months only where the penalty was imposed before the rules commenced.

Exam-safe point: Three months for a live case; six months only for pre-commencement penalties.

Statutory Authority: Rule 41(2) and (4), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Swapping the three-month and six-month periods

q: Where a servant is found unfit for further service, invalid pension may be granted:
opts: within six months of the medical certificate — Six months is not the period in rule 39(8)
within thirty days of the medical examination
within three months of the application for retirement
not later than forty five days from the date of receipt of the Format 6 certificate
expl:
( D) not later than forty five days from the date of receipt of the Format 6 certificate.
(B) within thirty days of the medical examination. — Thirty days is the period for requesting the examination under rule 39(3).
(C) within three months of the application for retirement. — The trigger is the certificate, and the period is forty-five days.

Rule 39(8) requires the medical authority to issue a Medical Certificate in Format 6 where the servant is found unfit for further service or fit only for less laborious work. Where he is found unfit, invalid pension may be granted under rule 44 not later than forty-five days from the date of receipt of that certificate. Rule 39(3) separately requires the Head of Office to request the examination within fifteen days and the examination to be held within thirty days.

Exam-safe point: Invalid pension: forty-five days from receipt of Format 6.

Statutory Authority: Rule 39(3) and (8), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Running the clock from the application instead of the certificate

q: A servant with 19 years and 10 months of qualifying service seeks voluntary retirement under rule 43. He:
opts: is eligible, since 19 years and 10 months rounds up to 20 years
is eligible if the appointing authority condones the shortfall
is not eligible, because the rule 44(7) rounding of three months or more does not apply to rule 43
is eligible only if he gives six months' notice
expl:
( C) is not eligible, because the rule 44(7) rounding of three months or more does not apply to rule 43.
(A) is eligible, since 19 years and 10 months rounds up to 20 years. — The fourth proviso expressly disapplies the rounding for rule 43.
(B) is eligible if the appointing authority condones the shortfall. — There is no condonation route in rule 43 for the twenty-year requirement.
(D) is eligible only if he gives six months' notice. — Notice length is not the obstacle; the qualifying service is.

Rule 43(1) allows voluntary retirement after twenty years' qualifying service on three months' notice. Its fourth proviso requires that the servant has completed, or will complete, twenty years on the intended date of retirement, and expressly disapplies rule 44(7), under which a fraction of three months or more is treated as a completed six-monthly period. Nineteen years and ten months therefore falls short, and the rule 44(8) concession of nine years and nine months is confined to pension on invalid retirement.

Exam-safe point: Twenty years exact for rule 43; no rounding under rule 44(7).

Statutory Authority: Rule 43(1) fourth proviso, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Importing rule 44(7) rounding into rule 43

q: Where the appointing authority relaxes the three-month notice under rule 43(4), the condition is that the servant:
opts: shall serve the balance of the notice after retirement — That would contradict the relaxation itself
shall not receive retirement gratuity until the notice period ends
shall not apply for commutation of a part of his pension before the expiry of the three-month notice period
shall forfeit one month's pension — No forfeiture of pension is prescribed
expl:
( C) shall not apply for commutation of a part of his pension before the expiry of the three-month notice period.
(B) shall not receive retirement gratuity until the notice period ends. — The bar in the rule is on commutation, not on gratuity.

Rule 43(4)(a) allows a request for acceptance of less than three months' notice with reasons; clause (b) lets the appointing authority relax the notice where the curtailment causes no administrative inconvenience, on the condition that the servant shall not apply for commutation of a part of his pension before the expiry of the three-month notice period. Commutation is governed by the CCS (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981 under rule 84(2).

Exam-safe point: Curtailed notice: no commutation until the three months would have run.

Statutory Authority: Rule 43(4)(b), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Missing the commutation condition attached to the relaxation

q: Which circumstance does NOT entitle the appointing authority to withhold permission to retire under rule 43?
opts: A charge sheet has been issued and disciplinary proceedings are pending
The servant has applied for an advance of pay
Judicial proceedings on charges of grave misconduct are pending
The servant is under suspension
expl:
( B) The servant has applied for an advance of pay.
(A) A charge sheet has been issued and disciplinary proceedings are pending. — Clause (ii) covers pending disciplinary proceedings.
(C) Judicial proceedings on charges of grave misconduct are pending. — Clause (iii) covers them, and the Explanation defines when they are pending.
(D) The servant is under suspension. — Clause (i) of rule 43(3) covers suspension.

Rule 43(3) allows permission to be withheld in three circumstances: suspension; a charge sheet issued with disciplinary proceedings pending; and judicial proceedings on charges which may amount to grave misconduct. The Explanation treats judicial proceedings as pending once a complaint or police report of which the Magistrate takes cognizance has been made. Even in those cases, the proviso permits acceptance with the approval of the President.

Exam-safe point: Three grounds for withholding; the President's approval can override them.

Statutory Authority: Rule 43(3) and its Explanation, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
src: Rule 43(3) and its Explanation, CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Inventing a fourth ground for withholding

q: A pensioner drawing a basic pension of ₹40,000 attains 92 years of age. His additional pension is:
opts: ₹16,000, being 40 per cent
₹12,000, being 30 per cent
₹40,000, being 100 per cent
₹20,000, being 50 per cent
expl:
( A) ₹16,000, being 40 per cent.
(B) ₹12,000, being 30 per cent. — Thirty per cent is the band for 85 to under 90 years.
(C) ₹40,000, being 100 per cent. — One hundred per cent is reached only at 100 years or more.
(D) ₹20,000, being 50 per cent. — Fifty per cent is the band for 95 to under 100 years.

Rule 44(6) pays additional pension by band: 20 per cent from 80 to under 85 years, 30 per cent from 85 to under 90, 40 per cent from 90 to under 95, 50 per cent from 95 to under 100, and 100 per cent at 100 years or more. At 92 the band is 40 per cent, which on a basic pension of ₹40,000 is ₹16,000. The additional pension is payable from the first day of the calendar month in which it falls due.

Exam-safe point: 92 years: the 40 per cent band.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(6)(a), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the 85-year or 95-year band

q: A servant retires with 27 years and 4 months of qualifying service. For rule 44 the service is reckoned as:
opts: 28 years
27 years exactly
27 years and 9 months
27 years and 6 months
expl:
( D) 27 years and 6 months.
(A) 28 years. — The rounding is to a six-monthly period, not to a whole year.
(B) 27 years exactly. — Four months is three months or more, so it becomes a completed six-monthly period.
(C) 27 years and 9 months. — The fraction becomes one six-monthly period, not two.

Rule 44(7) provides that in calculating the length of qualifying service a fraction of a year equal to three months and above is treated as a completed six-monthly period and reckoned as qualifying service. Four months reaches that threshold, so 27 years and 4 months is reckoned as 27 years and 6 months. Rule 44(8) makes a separate concession for nine years and nine months or more, treating it as ten years so that pension is payable at all.

Exam-safe point: Three months or more becomes a completed six-monthly period.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(7) and (8), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Rounding to a whole year, or dropping the fraction

q: A pension finally determined under rule 44 comes to ₹24,750.50. The amount payable is:
opts: ₹24,800, rounded to the nearest hundred
₹24,750.50, because pensions may be expressed in paise
expl:
( D) ₹24,751.
(A) ₹24,800, rounded to the nearest hundred. — There is no rounding to hundreds in the rule.
(B) ₹24,750. — The rule rounds to the next higher rupee, not to the nearest rupee.
(C) ₹24,750.50, because pensions may be expressed in paise. — Rule 44(9) requires expression in whole rupees.

Rule 44(9) requires the amount of pension, service gratuity, compassionate allowance, additional pension and additional compassionate allowance finally determined to be expressed in whole rupees, with any fraction of a rupee rounded off to the next higher rupee, separately for each amount. Rule 44(10) applies the same rounding to the pension payable for a fraction of a month where pension is discontinued mid-month.

Exam-safe point: Round up to the next rupee, separately for each amount.

Statutory Authority: Rule 44(9) and (10), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Rounding to the nearest rupee instead of upwards

q: A servant dies in service with 7 years of qualifying service and emoluments of ₹50,000. The death gratuity is:
expl:
( C) ₹6,00,000.
(A) ₹1,00,000. — That is the two-times rate for less than one year.
(B) ₹10,00,000. — That is the twenty-times rate, reached only at eleven years.
(D) ₹3,00,000. — That is the six-times rate for one year or more but less than five years.

Rule 45(1)(b) pays death gratuity by band: twice emoluments below one year, six times at one year or more but under five, twelve times at five years or more but under eleven, twenty times at eleven years or more but under twenty, and half of emoluments for every completed six-monthly period beyond twenty years, capped at thirty-three times. Seven years falls in the twelve-times band, so ₹50,000 gives ₹6,00,000.

Exam-safe point: Seven years: twelve times emoluments.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(1)(b), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Using the twenty-times band for a seven-year death

q: A servant retires, draws pension and retirement gratuity, and dies three years later. A residuary gratuity is payable where the sums he received:
opts: fall short of five years' pension
fall short of twelve times his emoluments, and the deficiency is then paid to his family
fall short of sixteen and a half times his emoluments
fall short of thirty-three times his emoluments — Thirty-three times is the cap on death gratuity
expl:
( B) fall short of twelve times his emoluments, and the deficiency is then paid to his family.
(A) fall short of five years' pension. — The comparison is with twelve times emoluments, not five years of pension.
(C) fall short of sixteen and a half times his emoluments. — Sixteen and a half times is the cap on retirement gratuity under rule 45(1)(a).

Rule 45(3) applies where a servant who became eligible for service gratuity or pension dies within five years of retirement, including compulsory retirement as a penalty, and the sums actually received by him on account of gratuity or pension, together with the retirement gratuity and the commuted value of any commuted portion, are less than twelve times his emoluments. A residuary gratuity equal to the deficiency is then paid to the family in the manner indicated in rule 47(1).

Exam-safe point: Residuary gratuity: top up to twelve times emoluments, within five years of retirement.

Statutory Authority: Rule 45(3), CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021
trap: Confusing the twelve-times residuary test with the gratuity caps

q: The death gratuity table in rule 45(1)(b) applies:
opts: also to the death of a Government servant by suicide
only to natural deaths
only if the servant had completed one year of qualifying service
only where the family establishes the death was attributable to service
expl:
( A) also to the death of a Government servant by suicide.
(B) only to natural deaths. — Rule 45(2) extends the table to suicide expressly.
(C) only if the servant had completed one year of qualifying service. — The table itself has a band for less than one year.
(D) only where the family establishes the death was attributable to service. — No such condition attaches to the death gratuity table.

Rule 45(2) states that the provision of clause (b) of sub-rule (1) shall also be applicable in the case of death of a Government servant by suicide.
